quote: Vielleicht die ersten Ziffern aus Stirlings Formel, und die letzten durch Congruenz-Rechnung.
english: Perhaps the first digits from Stirling's formula, and the last ones by congruence computation.
topic: Hilbert asks how the advantages of known arithmetic formulas (summation of arithmetic series, congruence formulas, Stirling's formula) for computing specific problems can be quantified by counting elementary operations, giving the digits of π and the computation of n! as examples.

triage.modern_statement: This is about how hard it is to compute pieces of n! for large n, counted in bit operations. (a) The leading k decimal digits of n! can be found from Stirling's asymptotic series for log Γ(n+1), using arithmetic at precision about k + log log n digits. That costs polylog(n) operations per fixed k, compared with roughly n log n bits just to write n! out in full. (b) The trailing digits can be found by congruence arithmetic, working with n! mod 10^k (or n! mod m). The last digits are trivially zeros: there are Σ⌊n/5^i⌋ of them. The real problem is the last k nonzero digits, which come from n!/10^v mod 10^k and can be computed by recursive congruence formulas. The broader question behind the note, how hard it is to compute n! or n! mod m in terms of elementary operations, became a question in algebraic and bit complexity theory.
triage.answered_by: No single person resolved it. The idea Hilbert sketches has become standard practice. Digits at the end: the last nonzero digits of n! follow fast congruence recursions, and their automaticity in a given base was studied in arXiv papers 1806.02560 and 1809.06947 (2018). Cost of the full factorial: Peter Borwein, 'On the complexity of calculating factorials', J. Algorithms 6 (1985) 376–380. Cost of n! mod p: Strassen and Pollard gave algorithms of roughly √n complexity, later improved by Bostan, Gaudry and Schost (SIAM J. Comput.). Whether n! has short straight-line programs is tied to the Shub–Smale τ-conjecture and the 'ultimate intractability' of n!. None of this was attributed to Hilbert, and the note is not one of his published problems.

evidence.claim: Borwein (1985) analysed the complexity of computing n! exactly.
The last nonzero digits of n! in a fixed base satisfy congruence recursions (e.g. ℓ_b of n! expressed via Euler's theorem mod b), and the resulting sequence is studied as an automatic sequence.
A further study covers the last nonzero digits of n! in a given base.
A simple recursion gives the last nonzero decimal digit of n! from D(floor(n/5)) and the unit digit of n, so it takes only O(log n) steps.
Strassen and Pollard showed n! mod p can be computed in about √n operations, and Bostan–Gaudry–Schost gave the best known classical method. Work on this continues.
Recent work tries to compute modular factorials faster than the square-root barrier.

The Shub–Smale τ-conjecture links the straight-line-program complexity of polynomials to their integer roots. It is connected to whether n! is 'ultimately hard' and has consequences for P vs NP in the Blum–Shub–Smale model.

triage.why: The note suggests a strategy: get the leading digits of n! from Stirling's formula and the trailing digits from congruences. Both halves are now standard and efficient. Stirling/log-gamma evaluation gives the leading digits, and modular recursions give the last nonzero digits; the trailing zeros themselves are trivial. In that narrow sense the idea is settled, which is why I chose 'solved', though no source says anyone confirmed it as a response to Hilbert. Hilbert's wider aim of quantifying how much a formula saves by counting elementary operations became complexity theory. Some of its factorial-specific questions are still open and actively studied: the true cost of n! mod p, which has no known polylog(n) algorithm, and the Shub–Smale question of whether n! is ultimately hard. I found no source linking this note to Hilbert's 23 problems or his 24th problem.
